summary: Describes version 2 of RPCSEC_GSS, which is the same as version 1 from RFC 2203 except that it adds support for channel bindings. RPCSEC_GSS lets remote procedure call protocols use the GSS-API for security. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7861.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a lock for the messages a program sends to another computer. The new version adds a way to tie the lock to the exact connection being used.

questions: how does rpcsec_gss v2 stop a man in the middle
subtitle: RPCSEC_GSS gains channel bindings, so RPC traffic can safely lean on an already-secure channel underneath.

tldr.problem: RPCSEC_GSS version 1 protects every RPC message with its own integrity or privacy processing, even when a lower layer such as IPsec already protects the connection.
tldr.mechanism: Version 2 adds one new procedure, RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL, in which both sides exchange GSS MICs over a hash of the channel bindings, and one new service, rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot, that skips per-message MICs once the channel is proven shared.
tldr.outcome: Everything else is identical to version 1. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2203 and was itself later updated by RFC 7861.

today: RFC 5403 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2203, and it has been updated by RFC 7861.

sections.title: Why Version 2 Exists
sections.content:
RFC 5403 describes RPCSEC_GSS version 2 (RPCSEC_GSSv2). It is the same as version 1, specified in RFC 2203, except that support for channel bindings has been added. RPCSEC_GSS lets remote procedure call (RPC) protocols use the Generic Security Services (GSS) framework.

The main motivation is to take advantage of hardware-assisted encryption that may exist lower in the stack, for example at the IP layer with IPsec. A second motivation is that, even without hardware help, encryption at a lower level can make RPCSEC_GSS-level encryption redundant.

GSS itself supports channel bindings, but not every implementation of every GSS mechanism does. That is why the RFC changes RPCSEC_GSS rather than relying on native GSS channel bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road is already guarded, you do not need a bodyguard for every package as well. This version lets the two sides check the road really is guarded.

sections.title: Channel Bindings Explained
sections.content:
A secure channel implies information shared by both ends, such as the concatenation of the public keys of the source and destination. The RFC uses this to defeat a man-in-the-middle (MITM). If a MITM sits between two parties there are two separate channels, and each uses different private keys, so the shared information cannot match on both.

RPCSEC_GSSv2 adds one optional round trip. The initiator computes a GSS MIC over the channel binding information and sends it to the target. The target verifies it and sends back its own MIC, which the initiator verifies.

That accomplishes three things at once: mutual authentication, proof that both sides know the channel's shared information (so they use the same channel), and both happening simultaneously. Once that is assured, the cost of computing MICs on every RPC request and reply can be dropped, because the channel does the same job.
sections.plainLanguage: Both of you whisper the same secret handshake, and each checks the other said it right. If a sneaky stranger were in the middle, the handshakes would not match.

sections.title: What Changes on the Wire
sections.content:
The RFC shows only the differences from version 1. Version 1 is fully supported by version 2. The credential keeps the same format as in version 1 (with the field renamed rgc_version so the XDR is legal), and setting rgc_version to 2 signals that the initiator and target support channel bindings.

Two enumerations each get one new value. rpc_gss_proc_t gains RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL = 4, and rpc_gss_service_t gains rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot = 4. The value 0 of the service enumeration is reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same form as before, with one extra tick box for the new handshake and one extra option for how carefully to wrap each message.

sections.title: The BIND_CHANNEL Procedure
sections.content:
Once an RPCSEC_GSSv2 handle has been established over a secure channel, the initiator MAY issue RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL. Targets MUST support it. Like the init requests, it uses the NULL RPC procedure, but its arguments are not overloaded, because the verifier is big enough. The service field is rpc_gss_svc_none, and seq_num is set as for a normal data request.

The request verifier is an XDR-encoded rgss2_bind_chan_verf_args with three fields: the channel binding prefix (up to, but excluding, the colon), the OID of the hash algorithm used, and a GSS MIC. The MIC covers the RPC header plus a hash of the channel bindings. A hash is used because some bindings, such as public keys, can be large.

The reply carries a status. RGSS2_BIND_CHAN_OK means the target accepted the bindings and verified the MIC. The other two statuses reject the request and return a list of what the target does support, so the initiator can pick its next preferred prefix or hash. The reply also carries a MIC over the sequence number, the hash and the result.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over a short fingerprint of the tunnel and sign it. The other side checks it and signs back, or tells you which kinds of fingerprints it likes better.

sections.title: The Channel Protection Service
sections.content:
Targets MUST support rpc_gss_svc_channel_prot. It is valid only when RPCSEC_GSSv2 is in use, a RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL has succeeded and the secure channel still exists.

With this service, requests and replies resemble those of rpc_gss_svc_none, except that the verifiers always have flavor AUTH_NONE and zero length. The credential is still non-NULL, and is the same one as before with the service field changed, so the principal can still be identified.

An initiator may, after a successful bind, map application requests for the none and integrity services to channel protection, and requests for privacy too if the channel has privacy enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: After the secret handshake, you stop signing each note. You only write your name on the envelope, because the tunnel already keeps notes safe.

sections.title: Version Negotiation and Deployment
sections.content:
An initiator that supports version 2 simply sends an RPCSEC_GSS request with rgc_version set to RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_2. A target that does not recognize it returns an RPC error as defined for version 1.

The initiator MUST NOT use a handle returned under version 2 with version 1 of the same target, nor the other way around. Implementations SHOULD NOT transfer tokens that use native GSS channel bindings, to ensure interoperability.

Because version 2 is a superset of version 1, it can be used wherever version 1 is. The RFC recommends it when channel bindings are desired or needed.
sections.plainLanguage: You just say which version you speak. If the other side does not know the new one, it says so. You must not mix the two kinds of passes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base considerations are those of RFC 2203, those of RFC 5056 (channel bindings) and those of the actual secure channel in use. The target SHOULD stop accepting channel-protected data requests once the GSS context expires.

Forging one MIC matters more here. In version 1 a forged MIC injects one bogus request. With version 2 plus channel bindings, one forged MIC lets an attacker inject requests for as long as the channel exists. The RFC describes a MITM that rewrites the version number and repeatedly tries to turn captured data MICs into a bind request.

Two defenses are given. The target SHOULD require a stronger MIC for a bind request than for data requests; for HMACs, log base 2 N bits longer when N data requests are expected. Also, after each failed bind MIC verification, the target SHOULD shorten the GSS context lifetime by a significant fraction. Halving it each time means a context with an 8 hour (28800 seconds) lifetime is destroyed after 15 failures.

Protecting the version number inside the init tokens was considered and rejected. It only moves the MIC guessing to the init message and cannot be done without changing GSS or the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thief could fake the handshake once, he could sneak in notes all day. So the guard asks for a longer password and gets stricter every time someone gets it wrong.

items.label: RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL
items.desc: New in version 2: binds the context to a secure channel.

messages.label: RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL
messages.note: Verifier holds the prefix, hash OID and a MIC over the RPC header and the hash of the channel bindings.

messages.label: Status + MIC
messages.note: OK, or a list of supported prefixes or hash algorithms, plus a MIC over the sequence number, hash and result.

items.label: RGSS2_BIND_CHAN_OK
items.desc: Channel bindings accepted and MIC verified.

items.desc: Prefix not supported; target lists the prefixes it supports.

items.desc: Hash algorithm not supported; target lists the OIDs it supports.
